title: Strings — Basic and Medium
relevance: String manipulation is a staple of SDE interviews and OAs, probing memory cost of copies, frequency counting, two pointers, and ASCII arithmetic.

phases.goal: Establish how C++ strings and characters behave, including append cost and ASCII arithmetic.

must_hit.point: std::string is a mutable dynamic array of char with fast random access and APIs like substr, find, and +=.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes string as a mutable char array and names common APIs such as substr, find, or +=.

must_hit.point: Building a string with s = s + c in a loop copies all characters each time and is O(n^2); use s += c or s.push_back(c) for amortized O(1) appends.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts quadratic reallocation/copy from + with amortized constant append via += or push_back.

must_hit.point: Characters are ASCII integers, so s[i] - 'a' maps lowercase letters to a 0-based alphabet index from 0 to 25.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains subtracting 'a' (or similar) to get alphabet indices in the 0..25 range.

must_hit.point: <cctype> provides utilities such as isalpha, isdigit, isalnum, tolower, and toupper.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names several of these character classification/case functions from <cctype>.

probes: What goes wrong if you build a string in a loop with s = s + c instead of s += c?
How do you map a lowercase letter to its alphabet index without a lookup table?

hints.1: Think about whether each append reuses the same buffer or builds a new string.
hints.2: Contrast full-string copy on every + with amortized append via += or push_back, and recall ASCII order of letters.
hints.3: s = s + c is O(n^2) because each step allocates and copies; s += c / push_back is amortized O(1); s[i] - 'a' gives indices 0 to 25.

phases.goal: Walk through core string algorithms: depth counters, two pointers, frequency maps, rotations, and center expansion.

must_hit.point: Remove outermost parentheses by tracking depth: append '(' only when depth > 0 before incrementing, and append ')' only when depth > 0 after decrementing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a depth counter and skipping parentheses that open at depth 0 or close back to 0.

must_hit.point: Largest odd number in a digit string: scan from the right for the first odd digit; the prefix through that digit is the answer (parity depends only on the last digit).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says scan right-to-left for an odd digit and return the prefix ending there.

must_hit.point: Longest common prefix: scan column by column across strings until a mismatch or the shortest string ends.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes vertical/index-aligned comparison across all strings stopping at first mismatch.

must_hit.point: Isomorphic strings need a bijection; track last-seen indices (e.g. size-256 arrays) and fail if current pair was last seen at different indices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions one-to-one mapping and comparing last-seen positions for both strings' characters.

must_hit.point: s is a rotation of goal iff lengths match and goal is a substring of s + s.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the doubled-string contains-all-rotations check with equal lengths.

must_hit.point: Anagrams: count frequencies in s and decrement for t (or equivalent); all counts must end at 0; sorting both is O(n log n) vs linear counting.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts sort-based check with a frequency count that resolves to zeros.

must_hit.point: atoi: skip spaces, read optional sign, accumulate digits; check overflow before result * 10 + digit using INT_MAX / 10 (and digit vs INT_MAX % 10), without relying on a wider type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes staged parsing and pre-multiply overflow guards against INT_MAX bounds.

must_hit.point: Longest palindromic substring via expand-around-center: try all 2n - 1 centers (odd and even) for O(n^2) time; brute force is O(n^3).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions expanding from odd and even centers totaling 2n - 1, beating cubic brute force.

must_hit.point: Roman to integer: add each value, but subtract when a smaller numeral precedes a larger one (e.g. IX is 9).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the subtractive rule by comparing a numeral to the next one.

probes: How would you check whether one string is a rotation of another without generating every shift?
Walk through how you prevent overflow in atoi without using a type wider than 32-bit.
How does expand-around-center find the longest palindromic substring?

hints.1: For rotations, think about what substrings appear if you concatenate the string with itself.
hints.2: For atoi, compare the running total to INT_MAX / 10 before multiplying; for palindromes, expand from both character and between-character centers.
hints.3: Equal length and goal in s+s; overflow check before *10; 2n - 1 centers give O(n^2) vs O(n^3) brute force.

phases.goal: Surface when to prefer in-place updates, fixed alphabet arrays, and algorithm complexity choices on strings.

must_hit.point: For limited alphabets (e.g. lowercase), a fixed array like int freq[26] is faster and uses less memory than std::unordered_map.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Prefers a size-26 (or constant alphabet) array over a hash map for frequency problems.

must_hit.point: Interviewers weigh memory efficiency: copying strings in loops versus O(1) in-place modifications via references or pointer-style edits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Discusses avoiding repeated string copies in favor of in-place or constant-extra-space edits.

must_hit.point: Rotate-string find on s+s is O(n^2) with standard library find, or O(n) with KMP; reverse-words optimal path is O(n) time and O(1) space in place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions find vs KMP cost and/or in-place reverse-words complexity.

must_hit.point: Palindromic substring: O(n^3) brute, O(n^2) expand-around-center, O(n) Manacher (advanced); beauty-of-substrings needs O(n^2) enumeration with a 26-slot freq window.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders palindrome approaches by complexity and notes O(n^2) beauty enumeration with fixed freq size.

probes: When would you use int freq[26] instead of an unordered_map in a string problem?
What complexity tradeoffs exist between brute force, expand-around-center, and Manacher for longest palindromic substring?

hints.1: Consider alphabet size and constant overhead of hashing.
hints.2: Fixed small alphabets favor arrays; palindrome search can escalate from checking all substrings to center expansion to Manacher.
hints.3: freq[26] beats unordered_map for lowercase; palindrome is O(n^3) brute, O(n^2) centers, O(n) Manacher.

phases.goal: Apply string patterns to representative problems: parentheses depth, word reversal, frequency sort, and related OA staples.

must_hit.point: Maximum nesting depth of parentheses: increment on '(', decrement on ')', track the maximum current depth in one O(n) pass with O(1) space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes a running depth counter and taking its maximum over the scan.

must_hit.point: Reverse words in a string (order of words): reverse the whole string, then reverse each word token; complexity O(n) time, O(1) space when done in place.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States whole-string reverse then per-word reverse, emphasizing in-place linear work.

must_hit.point: Reverse every word in place while preserving word order: scan for spaces as boundaries and reverse each word window.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains finding word boundaries and reversing characters within each word only.

must_hit.point: Sort characters by frequency: count occurrences, then sort unique characters by count (or bucket/priority queue); time O(n log k) with k unique characters (k ≤ 256).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes frequency count then sorting/bucketing by frequency, citing O(n log k) with bounded k.

must_hit.point: Sum of beauty of all substrings: for each start, extend end while maintaining a frequency array and add max_freq - min_nonzero_freq each step.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes nested start/end loops with a running freq map and beauty as max minus nonzero min.

probes: How do you compute maximum nesting depth of a valid parentheses string in linear time?
Explain an in-place approach to reverse the order of words in a string.
How would you sum the beauty of all substrings efficiently enough for an OA?

hints.1: Parentheses depth is just a counter; word-order reversal often uses multiple reverse passes.
hints.2: Reverse the entire string then each word; for beauty, fix start and grow end with a frequency window.
hints.3: Track max depth on '('; reverse-all then reverse-tokens for word order; O(n^2) start/end with freq[26] for beauty.

tradeoffs.topic: s = s + c vs s += c / push_back
tradeoffs.strong_answer: s = s + c rebuilds and copies the whole string each iteration (O(n^2)); s += c or push_back appends in amortized O(1).
For limited alphabets like lowercase letters, a fixed array is dramatically faster and uses less memory than a hash map.

tradeoffs.topic: Anagram via sorting vs frequency counting
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Sorting both strings is O(n log n); counting frequencies and checking all counts reach 0 is linear time with O(1) space for a constant alphabet.

tradeoffs.topic: Reverse words: word array vs in-place reverses
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Extracting words into an array then reversing is simple but uses extra space; trimming, reversing the whole string, then reversing each token achieves O(n) time and O(1) space in place.

tradeoffs.topic: Rotate check: library find vs KMP
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Checking if goal is in s+s via standard find is O(n^2); KMP can make the substring search O(n), with O(n) space for the concatenated string.

tradeoffs.topic: Longest palindromic substring: brute vs expand vs Manacher
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Brute checking all substrings is O(n^3); expand-around-center over 2n - 1 centers is O(n^2); Manacher is O(n) but advanced.

tradeoffs.topic: atoi overflow: long long clamp vs pre-check on 32-bit int
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Accumulating in long long then clamping is often disallowed; check against INT_MAX / 10 (and the last digit bound) before multiplying and adding on a 32-bit result.

gotchas.trap: Building a result with s = s + c inside a loop.
gotchas.correction: Use s += c or s.push_back(c) so each append is amortized O(1), not O(n^2) full copies.

gotchas.trap: Implementing atoi by accumulating into a long long and clamping only at the end.
gotchas.correction: Interviewers often forbid wider-than-32-bit types; detect overflow before result * 10 + digit using INT_MAX / 10 (and INT_MAX % 10 for the edge digit).

gotchas.trap: Using std::unordered_map for lowercase-only frequency problems by default.
gotchas.correction: Prefer a fixed int freq[26] (or similar constant alphabet array) for better time and memory constants.

gotchas.trap: Treating isomorphic strings as only a one-way map from s to t.
gotchas.correction: A bijection is required; last-seen index arrays (size 256) on both sides catch when two characters would map inconsistently.
